scenario: AITA for Seeking Prayers at a Scheduled Prayer Service? | Hello all. This week I was at a prayer service at my college fellowship. We have these once a week, and they are open to the public. A student at our school died recently in an accident, and so there were more people at the service than normal. Lots of people were crying. I did not know him, but I still prayed for him with everyone else. During the service, people offer up statements and some ask for prayers. This time, lots of people were remembering the student but a few people asked for prayers for sick relatives, one for her cousin who was struggling with drug addiction, and then it came to me. I broke up with my girlfriend of about 3 months two weeks ago, and it has been really tough on me. She was also at the prayer service even though she is not as Christian as I am and normally was not there. She just happened to know the student who passed away. I asked people to pray for me that I recover from my breakup and that in the future I only date people who truly share my religious values because those people would not be hurtful. Fast forward to that afternoon, I got messages from several of my friends telling me that asking for prayers, during a prayer service, was inconsiderate. My ex girlfriend also sent me a message telling me that she found it hurtful and that she would prefer that I not speak about her again, at least not when she is present. I asked her what was wrong with what I said, and she told me I was attacking her. I was not! I never attacked her. I understand that people there were suffering, but we all suffer for different reasons. I am also suffering. I have never had such a tragic breakup, and I thought she was the one who I would marry. I was already looking at rings, and then she just broke up with me. I have a right to be sad, don't I? I have a right to ask to be lifted in spirit--we all have different crosses to bear. A couple of my friends are not even talking to me. Am I really wrong here? I am interested in what you have to say.

Let me break this down step by step. First, the scenario is that a student attended a prayer service at their college fellowship. The service was more crowded than usual because a student had recently died in an accident. Many people were there to remember him, and some were asking for prayers for other issues, like sick relatives or a cousin struggling with addiction. Then it came to the person in question, who broke up with their girlfriend two weeks ago after three months. They asked for prayers to recover from the breakup and to date people who share their religious values. After the service, several friends told him it was inconsiderate, and his ex-girlfriend said she found it hurtful and asked him not to speak about her again, especially when she's present. He's confused because he feels he has a right to be sad and to ask for spiritual support. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong for him to ask for prayers in that setting? I think I need to consider a few factors here. First, the context of the prayer service. It was organized to remember a student who died, so the primary focus was on that tragedy. However, prayer services are generally open to anyone who needs support, regardless of the reason. So, in that sense, asking for prayers for a breakup might be appropriate because it's a form of personal suffering. But then, why did his friends and ex-girlfriend find it inconsiderate? Maybe because the primary purpose of the service was to remember the deceased student. By bringing up his breakup, he might have diverted attention away from the main reason people were there. It could have been seen as self-centered, especially since others were dealing with more significant losses. Another angle is the presence of his ex-girlfriend. She wasn't a regular attendee but was there because she knew the deceased student. By asking for prayers related to their breakup, he might have brought up painful memories for her, especially if she was still emotionally involved or if the breakup was recent. She might have felt that her presence was being used as a platform for his personal issues, which could be hurtful. Additionally, the way he phrased his prayer might have been interpreted as attacking her. He mentioned wanting to date people who share his religious values, implying that his ex-girlfriend didn't, which could have come off as critical or judgmental. That could explain why she felt attacked. On the other hand, he feels he has a right to express his pain and seek support. It's valid to feel sad after a breakup, and seeking communal prayer can be a way to find comfort and guidance. However, the setting and the audience matter. In a service focused on a specific tragedy, it might be more appropriate to focus on that unless others have already opened the door to broader prayer requests. I also need to consider the Christian perspective. In many Christian traditions, prayer services are inclusive and meant for all who are in need. However, there's also an emphasis on being considerate of others' feelings and not causing unnecessary pain. The Bible teaches about love, compassion, and putting others first. So, while it's okay to seek prayer, it should be done in a way that doesn't make others uncomfortable or feel attacked. In this case, the person might have been right in seeking prayer but perhaps went about it in a way that was insensitive to the context and the presence of his ex-girlfriend. It's possible that he didn't consider how his request might affect others, especially someone who was directly involved in his personal issue. So, putting it all together, while seeking prayer is a valid and right thing to do, the manner and context in which it's done matter. In this scenario, the person might have been right in seeking prayer but wrong in how and where they did it, leading to hurt feelings and misunderstandings.
